Foreword and Hope

There is no specific message intended to be conveyed via this page outside of the fact that there have been an popular existentially heavy meme in early 2026 about a penguin facing the mountains.
The penguin famously chose voluntarily death.
Many people including myself were deeply affected by it.
This served as an inspiration.

I hope there is a heaven for penguins as well.

Database and Preview

This site will employ Sqlite3 to make real SQL work possible in a Quarto Project.

Code 
# Opening sqlite3 for a new database.
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('data/AllCounts_V_4_4.csv')
conn = sqlite3.connect('data/penguins_sights.db')

# Moving data to the DB for the flatfile source
# Priority for this page has been to keep the data managable and and the database quarto applicable
#learning the to work via cursor is the main takeaway with this site
c = conn.cursor()
# basics of the database
x = c.execute("SELECT name, type FROM sqlite_master;")

# checking the objects in the database
objects = x.fetchall()

for name, type in objects:
        print(f"I found a {type} called: {name}")

df.to_sql('observations', conn, if_exists='replace',index=False)
I found a table called: observations
5407

The attributes are available in the below table. Apparently there no forced not nulls, nor foreign keys present. Since a sole table is loaded into the database, no relational connections are built. Easy to target the penguin_count as a fact to be measured in the following visualizations.
The table could be considered ‘business’ ready for inquiry and analysis.
I intend to run some basic SQL queries which will prepare the right data format for the visualizations.

Observations over Time and Space

For the sake of simplicity I am selecting 20 records in a pseudorandom order. In a real data inquiry, we would need a specified set of criteria, which islands - dates - types etc should be considered and compared.

Code 
# getting the first and last years and the number of observations
# removing 'Anvers' for chart aesthetics
q_sites_obs_range = """SELECT site_id
      ,site_name
      ,min(season_starting) AS "First observation year"
      ,max(season_starting) AS "Last observation year"
      ,max(season_starting) - min(season_starting)+1 AS "Observation range in years"
      ,count(season_starting) AS "Number of observations"
      FROM observations 
      GROUP BY 
      site_id
      ,site_name
      HAVING site_name not like '%Anvers%'
      ORDER BY rowid * 1235 % 897
      LIMIT 20;"""
      
df_sites_obs_range= pd.read_sql(q_sites_obs_range, conn)

import plotly.express as px

fig = px.bar(
        df_sites_obs_range,
        x='Observation range in years',
        y='site_name',
        base='First observation year',
        orientation='h',
        color='Number of observations',
        title='Observation Counts per Sites over Ranges',
        labels={"site_name": "Site Name"}
        )
fig.update_layout(
        height=800,
        width=1200,
        coloraxis_colorbar=dict(
                title="Number of Observations",
                thicknessmode="pixels",
                thickness=15,
                orientation="h",
        ),
        xaxis_title='<b>Observation range years</b>',
        yaxis_title='<b>Site name</b>',
        template="simple_white",
        margin=dict(l=20,r=20,t=40, b=100)
)
fig.show()


Boxplotting the number of observations highlight the underlying distribution. Clearly saturation of the observations vary greatly which is always a risk for premature conclusions.
One site is well observed but 50 percent of the observations range between 1.5 and 9.5. In itself a huge range. This could point the reader to the fact that most sites are barely observed so do not have solid data to see the population dynamics.
Also there are both spatial and the temporal count_type variatons present, and I am sure there should be a biologically significant factor of the penguin subspecies as well.
Therefore, this dataset is rather just raw glimpse into the penguin locations. This is actually a good point to highlight that oftentimes the job of the data analysis is to clearly set the limitations of the dataset, to avoid false conlusions.

The below visualization will balance the variations slightly. Only the last observation years are present and for all of the sites. Therefore we meaningfully observe the population spatially, although not temporally. Altough qualitative domain knowledge is always a prerequisit for real data analyis.

Code 
# Selecting the last observation of each site for count visualization
q_last_number_pingi = """WITH last_obs AS (
        SELECT site_id
        ,site_name
        ,longitude_epsg_4326
        ,latitude_epsg_4326
        ,season_starting
       --,printf('%04d-%02d-%02d', year, month,day) AS "DATE"
      ,penguin_count
      ,ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY SITE_ID ORDER BY year DESC, month DESC, day DESC) AS "RN"
      FROM observations)
      SELECT lo.site_id,
      lo.site_name,
      lo.season_starting,
      lo.longitude_epsg_4326,
      lo.latitude_epsg_4326,
      lo.penguin_count 
      FROM last_obs lo 
      WHERE lo.RN = 1;"""

df_last_number_pingi = pd.read_sql(q_last_number_pingi, conn)

# changing numbers to whole number
df_last_number_pingi['penguin_count']= df_last_number_pingi['penguin_count'].astype('Int64')

df_last_number_pingi = df_last_number_pingi.astype({
        'site_id': 'category',
        'site_name': 'category',
        'season_starting': 'category'
})

import pydeck as pdk

layer = pdk.Layer(
        "HexagonLayer",
        data= df_last_number_pingi,
        get_position=["longitude_epsg_4326","latitude_epsg_4326"],
        auto_highlight=True,
        elevation_scale=50,
        pickable=True,
        elevation_range=[0, 3000],
        extruded=True,
        coverage=1
)

view_state= pdk.ViewState(
        latitude= -64.737905,
        longitude= -63.896758,
        zoom=4,
        pitch=45,
        bearing=0
)
#Render 
r = pdk.Deck(layers=[layer], initial_view_state=view_state)
r.to_html("hexagon_map.html")

In the last chart, two variables will be controlled. Only nests will be shown for one given type of penguins with will be the chinstraps.
Lastly only those sites will be shown that had at least 30 observations have happened.

Code 
import plotly.express as px

# those sites where there have been at least 20 observations

more_than_twenty = """
      SELECT o.site_id,
      o.site_name,
      o.season_starting,
      --o.longitude_epsg_4326,
      --o.latitude_epsg_4326,
      o.penguin_count,
      o.common_name
      FROM observations o 
      WHERE common_name='chinstrap penguin' and count_type='nests'  and o.site_id in (
      WITH cte_count AS (SELECT site_id
      ,count(site_id) AS "COUNT_OBV"
      FROM observations
      WHERE common_name='chinstrap penguin' and count_type='nests' 
      GROUP BY site_id)
      select site_id from cte_count where COUNT_OBV > 30);"""

df_more_than_twenty = pd.read_sql(more_than_twenty, conn)
df_more_than_twenty

# linechart
fig_line = px.line(
        df_more_than_twenty,
        x='season_starting',
        y='penguin_count',
        title='Change of Nests for Chinstrap Penguins With More Than 60 Observations',
        color='site_name',
        template='plotly_white'
)

fig_line.update_layout(
        legend = dict(
                orientation= "h",
                yanchor = "bottom"
                )
)

fig_line.show()

Apparently focusing this subset, now the temporal effects are clearly visible. We can now deduct meaningful observations both spatially and temporally.
This is finally now a controlled objective conclusion given the data are correct. Cape Shireff and Half Moon Island are counting much higher populations which make the Y axis for the other sites less visible. Nonetheless the number of nests are trending down in all observed locations. But Why?

Have I had experience in the domain of this branch of biology might I assume ‘reason’-s or dynamics, or asked for further questions.
The actual work on the real world could start there.
